claim: Proliferating animal cells maintain a stable size distribution over generations despite fluctuations in cell growth and division size.
source: Proliferating animal cells maintain a stable size distribution over generations despite fluctuations in cell growth and division size.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell biology that is part of the study's background and motivation.

claim: Cell size control involves both cell size checkpoints, which delay cell cycle progression in small cells, and size-dependent regulation of mass accumulation rates.
source: Previously, we showed that cell size control involves both cell size checkpoints, which delay cell cycle progression in small cells, and size-dependent regulation of mass accumulation rates (Ginzberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The p38 MAPK pathway is a key regulator of the mammalian cell size checkpoint.
source: While we previously identified the p38 MAPK pathway as a key regulator of the mammalian cell size checkpoint (Liu et al., 2018), the mechanism of size-dependent growth rate regulation has remained elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Protein synthesis rates scale proportionally with cell size across cell cycle stages and experimental conditions.
source: We found that protein synthesis rates scale proportionally with cell size across cell cycle stages and experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Oversized cells that undergo compensatory growth slowdown exhibit a superlinear increase in proteasome-mediated protein degradation.
source: In contrast, oversized cells that undergo compensatory growth slowdown exhibit a superlinear increase in proteasome-mediated protein degradation, with accelerated protein turnover per unit mass, suggesting activation of the proteasomal degradation pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Both nascent and long-lived proteins contribute to the elevated protein degradation during compensatory growth slowdown.
source: Both nascent and long-lived proteins contribute to the elevated protein degradation during compensatory growth slowdown, with long-lived proteins playing a crucial role at the G1/S transition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Large G1/S cells exhibit particularly high efficiency in protein degradation, surpassing that of similarly sized or larger cells in S and G2.
source: Notably, large G1/S cells exhibit particularly high efficiency in protein degradation, surpassing that of similarly sized or larger cells in S and G2, coinciding with the timing of the most stringent size control in animal cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Oversized cells reduce their growth efficiency by activating global proteasome-mediated protein degradation to promote cell size homeostasis.
source: These results collectively suggest that oversized cells reduce their growth efficiency by activating global proteasome-mediated protein degradation to promote cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Stringent regulation of cell size exists in wide-ranging systems such as single-celled yeasts, animal cells in culture and within tissues, as well as plant meristem cells.
source: This stringent regulation of cell size exists in wide-ranging systems such as single-celled yeasts (Hartwell et al., 1974; Johnston et al., 1977; Nurse, 1975; Schmoller et al., 2015), animal cells in culture and within tissues (Ginzberg et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Xie and Skotheim, 2020; Zatulovskiy et al., 2020), as well as plant meristem cells (D'Ario et al., 2021; Serrano-Mislata et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Misregulation of cell size control results in increased size heterogeneity, which is typically observed during neoplastic growth and is a hallmark of malignancy in many tumors.
source: Misregulation of cell size control results in increased size heterogeneity, which is typically observed during neoplastic growth and is a hallmark of malignancy in many tumors, including breast cancer and small cell lung cancer (Asadullah et al., 2021; Bell and Waizbard, 1986; Ginzberg et al., 2015; Lee et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The mammalian G1/S cell size checkpoint was first reported by Zetterberg and Killander over 50 years ago.
source: The mammalian G1/S cell size checkpoint was first reported by Zetterberg and Killander over 50 years ago (Killander and Zetterberg, 1965; Zetterberg and Killander, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical work.

claim: Similar size checkpoints have been identified in single-celled yeasts.
source: Subsequently, similar size checkpoints have been identified in single-celled yeasts (Hartwell et al., 1974; Nurse, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Smaller cells spend longer periods of growth in G1, allowing cells to reach the target size as they transition into S phase.
source: With increased resolution, these newer studies directly confirmed that smaller cells spend longer periods of growth in G1, allowing cells to reach the target size as they transition into S phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from cited studies.

claim: Studies have revealed roles for both the p38 MAPK and the CDK4/Rb pathways in animal cell size sensing.
source: Although it is not yet clear how animal cells sense their size, studies have revealed roles for both the p38 MAPK (Liu et al., 2018; Sellam et al., 2019) and the CDK4/Rb pathways (Datar et al., 2000; Tan et al., 2021; Zatulovskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Mammalian cells employ size-dependent regulation of cellular growth rate.
source: In addition to cell size checkpoints, two independent studies suggest that mammalian cells also employ size-dependent regulation of cellular growth rate (Cadart et al., 2018; Ginzberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The rate of cell growth negatively correlated with cell size at various cell cycle stages.
source: Authors of the studies used different methods to measure the growth of individual cell size throughout the cell cycle and found that the rate of cell growth negatively correlated with cell size at various cell cycle stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cells under CDK2 inhibition were forced to grow for a longer period in G1, resulting in an immediate increase in cell size.
source: For example, cells under CDK2 inhibition were forced to grow for a longer period in G1, resulting in an immediate increase in cell size.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells later compensated for the longer period of growth with slower rates of mass accumulation, resulting in only a small increase in cell size.
source: Remarkably, cells later compensated for this longer period of growth with slower rates of mass accumulation, resulting in only a small increase in cell size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CDK4/6 inhibition does not trigger compensatory growth slowdown.
source: Notably, this compensation does not occur with CDK4/6 inhibition (Ginzberg et al., 2018), which was found to reprogram cells to a larger target size (see Tan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Proteasome-mediated global protein degradation, rather than protein synthesis, underlies the size-dependent compensatory growth.
source: We found that proteasome-mediated global protein degradation, rather than protein synthesis, underlies the size-dependent compensatory growth and functions in parallel with cell size checkpoints to promote cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CDK2 inhibition resulted in a longer G1 phase (+3.5 hr, 32%) and lower growth rates of nuclear size (–21%).
source: Consistent with results from the fixed cell assay, CDK2 inhibition resulted in a longer G1 phase (+3.5 hr, 32%) and lower growth rates of nuclear size (–21%) (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B–E.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells had a larger initial size as a result of prolonged growth duration from the previous cycle.
source: Although CDK2-inhibited cells had a larger initial size as a result of prolonged growth duration from the previous cycle, they grew slower and became similarly sized as control cells around the G1/S transition, which was apparent when growth trajectories were computationally synchronized to the timing of their G1/S transition (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells grew slower and became similarly sized as control cells around the G1/S transition.
source: Although CDK2-inhibited cells had a larger initial size as a result of prolonged growth duration from the previous cycle, they grew slower and became similarly sized as control cells around the G1/S transition, which was apparent when growth trajectories were computationally synchronized to the timing of their G1/S transition (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells initially grew at the same rate as control but later compensated with a 24% reduced rate of mass accumulation.
source: This revealed that CDK2-inhibited cells initially grew at the same rate as control but later compensated with a 24% reduced rate of mass accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rates of cell proliferation remained unchanged (25% lower than control) throughout the CDK2 inhibition experiment.
source: In comparison, rates of cell proliferation remained unchanged (25% lower than control) throughout the experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Ginzberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: The delayed compensatory slowdown in cellular growth suggests that the influence of CDK2 inhibitor on growth rate is indirect and is mediated by a property that accumulates over time, presumably cell size.
source: The delayed compensatory slowdown in cellular growth suggests that the influence of CDK2 inhibitor on growth rate is indirect and is mediated by a property that accumulates over time, presumably cell size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Proteins represent more than half of the cell's total dry mass in an actively proliferating mammalian cell.
source: In an actively proliferating mammalian cell, proteins represent more than half of the cell's total dry mass (Mitchison, 1971) and are under active turnover (Ghenim et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Total protein content linearly scales with the dry mass and volume of cells at different cell cycle stages.
source: Total protein content also linearly scales with the dry mass and volume of cells at different cell cycle stages (Berenson et al., 2019; Kafri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The balance between protein translation and degradation has been shown to significantly influence cell size in various cell types.
source: The balance between protein translation and degradation has been shown to significantly influence cell size in various cell types, including neurons, muscles, and cancer cells (Acebron et al., 2014; Franklin and Johnson, 1998; Gordon et al., 2013; Sandri, 2013), suggesting a vital role of protein homeostasis in cell size control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Treating cells with the protein synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide (CHX), significantly reduces AHA incorporation.
source: Treating cells with the protein synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide (CHX), significantly reduces AHA incorporation (Figure 2A), confirming the efficacy of the assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: In unperturbed cells, AHA incorporation levels positively correlated with total protein content (R = 0.91).
source: In unperturbed cells, AHA incorporation levels positively correlated with total protein content (R = 0.91) (Figure 2A), indicating a faster rate of protein synthesis in large cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The dependence of AHA incorporation on size was consistent for G1, S, and G2 cells.
source: To test if the positive correlation between cell size and AHA incorporation is cell cycle dependent, we further segregated cells by their cell cycle stage and found that the dependence of AHA incorporation on size was consistent for G1, S, and G2 cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Larger cells incorporated more AHA per unit time in all cell cycle stages.
source: In all cell cycle stages, larger cells incorporated more AHA per unit time.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The linear dependence of AHA incorporation on cell size persists across a wide range of sizes, even for cells that are approximately twofold larger, as induced by CDK4/6 inhibition.
source: Markedly, the linear dependence of AHA incorporation on cell size persists across a wide range of sizes, even for cells that are approximately twofold larger, as induced by CDK4/6 inhibition (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells demonstrated a slight increase in both cell size (~11%) and AHA incorporation (~4%) compared to that of control.
source: CDK2-inhibited cells demonstrated a slight increase in both cell size (~11%) and AHA incorporation (~4%) compared to that of control (Figure 2C), despite the compensatory slowdown of growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells maintained a similar linear correlation between cell size and AHA incorporation, both at the single-cell level and across different cell cycle stages.
source: Consistent with measurements in unperturbed cells, CDK2-inhibited cells maintained a similar linear correlation between cell size and AHA incorporation, both at the single-cell level and across different cell cycle stages (Figure 2B and C), suggesting that the protein synthesis machinery is not affected by CDK2 inhibition throughout the duration of the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The compensatory growth slowdown in CDK2-inhibited cells is not mediated through a decrease in overall rates of protein synthesis but likely through an increase in overall protein degradation.
source: Together, results from the AHA pulse experiments suggest that the compensatory growth slowdown in CDK2-inhibited cells is not mediated through a decrease in overall rates of protein synthesis but likely through an increase in overall protein degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Significantly increased rates of protein degradation were observed in larger cells (80th percentile) compared to smaller cells (20th percentile).
source: Interestingly, we observed significantly increased rates of protein degradation in larger cells (80th percentile) compared to smaller cells (20th percentile) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the hypothesis that large cells may activate global protein degradation to initiate a compensatory growth slowdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proteasome-mediated protein degradation is a major route of protein turnover in non-starved cells.
source: Proteasome-mediated protein degradation is a major route of protein turnover in non-starved cells (Lecker et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The major targeting signal for proteasomal degradation is a post-translational modification involving ubiquitin chains linked through Lysine 48 (K48).
source: The major targeting signal for proteasomal degradation is a post-translational modification involving ubiquitin chains linked through Lysine 48 (K48) (Yau and Rape, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cell size and the partitioning of cells into different cell cycle stages were not significantly influenced by the 30 min treatment with CFZ.
source: Cell size and the partitioning of cells into different cell cycle stages were not significantly influenced by the 30 min treatment with CFZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells showed higher rates of ΔK48-polyUb, affirming a role of proteasomes in compensatory growth.
source: CDK2-inhibited cells showed higher rates of ΔK48-polyUb, affirming a role of proteasomes in compensatory growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells had similar ΔK48-polyUb as control during the first 8 hr of treatment, but later showed a significant increase in ΔK48-polyUb at 24 hr.
source: CDK2-inhibited cells had similar ΔK48-polyUb as control during the first 8 hr of treatment, but later showed a significant increase in ΔK48-polyUb at 24 hr, indicating increased rates of protein degradation (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The enhanced turnover of K48-polyUb proteins aligns temporally with the compensatory growth rate changes observed in CDK2-inhibited cells.
source: The enhanced turnover of K48-polyUb proteins aligns temporally with the compensatory growth rate changes observed in CDK2-inhibited cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The pattern of increased ΔK48-polyUb was consistently observed across G1, S, and G2+M phases in CDK2-inhibited cells.
source: This pattern was consistently observed across G1, S, and G2+M phases in CDK2-inhibited cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The delayed kinetics suggest that the increased ΔK48-polyUb is not triggered by the immediate inhibition of CDK2 activity but rather from the buildup of excessive cell mass triggered by the gradual influence of the longer cell cycle.
source: The delayed kinetics suggest that the increased ΔK48-polyUb is not triggered by the immediate inhibition of CDK2 activity but rather from the buildup of excessive cell mass triggered by the gradual influence of the longer cell cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The compensatory slowdown of cell growth is mediated by increased clearance of K48-polyUb.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the compensatory slowdown of cell growth is mediated by increased clearance of K48-polyUb.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Perturbation of CDK2 activity promotes proportional increases in both cell size and the rate of AHA incorporation across all cell cycle stages.
source: Perturbation of CDK2 activity promotes proportional increases in both cell size and the rate of AHA incorporation across all cell cycle stages (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells exhibit disproportionately larger changes in protein degradation (ΔK48-polyUb) relative to the changes in cell size, suggesting a superlinear relationship.
source: However, CDK2-inhibited cells exhibit disproportionately larger changes in protein degradation (ΔK48-polyUb) relative to the changes in cell size, suggesting a superlinear relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: ΔK48-polyUb increased by ~30% in CDK2-inhibited cells, whereas mean cell size only increased by ~3.4% compared to control.
source: On average, ΔK48-polyUb increased by ~30% in CDK2-inhibited cells, whereas mean cell size only increased by ~3.4% compared to control (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The disproportionate increase in degradation rates was consistent across all interphase stages (G1: 44%; S: 42%; G2+M: 31%).
source: This disproportionate increase in degradation rates was consistent across all interphase stages (G1: 44%; S: 42%; G2+M: 31%) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Larger cells have higher rates of protein synthesis, but the rates of AHA incorporation per unit cell mass remain relatively constant across different cell sizes.
source: Although larger cells have higher absolute rates of protein synthesis, the rates of AHA incorporation per unit cell mass remain relatively constant across different cell sizes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Larger cells have higher rates of protein degradation even when quantified per unit cellular mass, suggesting an activation of the protein degradation pathways in large cells.
source: In contrast, larger cells have higher rates of protein degradation even when quantified per unit cellular mass, suggesting an activation of the protein degradation pathways in large cells, in addition to large cells having more proteins to degrade.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: CDK4/6 inhibition resulted in significant increases in both cell size (G1: 32%; S: 69%; G2+M: 38%) and ΔK48-polyUb (G1: 30%; S: 66%; G2+M: 45%) at 24 hr of treatment.
source: As expected, CDK4/6 inhibition resulted in significant increases in both cell size (G1: 32%; S: 69%; G2+M: 38%) and ΔK48-polyUb (G1: 30%; S: 66%; G2+M: 45%) at 24 hr of treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The increases in ΔK48-polyUb under CDK4/6 inhibition remained proportional to the changes in cell size.
source: However, the increases in ΔK48-polyUb remained proportional to the changes in cell size.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cell size and ΔK48-polyUb under CDK4/6 inhibition followed the same linear relationship as control cells across different cell cycle stages.
source: Unlike the superlinear increase in ΔK48-polyUb observed in CDK2-inhibited cells (Figure 3D), cell size and ΔK48-polyUb under CDK4/6 inhibition followed the same linear relationship as control cells across different cell cycle stages (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Compensatory degradation is not triggered merely by shifts in target size.
source: This suggests that compensatory degradation is not triggered merely by shifts in target size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: JNJ-26854165 slows S phase progression and barasertib delays mitosis.
source: Using data from a previous in-house chemical screen (Kaufman et al., 2022), we identified compounds that increase cell size by altering progression rates of different cell cycle stages: JNJ-26854165, which slows S phase progression, and barasertib, which delays mitosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and citation to previous work.

claim: Both JNJ-26854165 and barasertib led to increased global protein degradation, as measured by ΔK48-polyUb.
source: Both compounds led to increased global protein degradation, as measured by ΔK48-polyUb (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: JNJ-26854165 and barasertib induced disproportionately higher increases in ΔK48-polyUb relative to the cell size increases, particularly in the affected cell cycle stages.
source: Similar to the effects of CDK2 inhibition, they induced disproportionately higher increases in ΔK48-polyUb relative to the cell size increases, particularly in the affected cell cycle stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Barasertib-treated G2+M cells exhibited a 10% increase in cell size but a 37% increase in ΔK48-polyUb at 8 hr of treatment.
source: Barasertib-treated G2+M cells exhibited a 10% increase in cell size but a 37% increase in ΔK48-polyUb at 8 hr of treatment, and the superlinear increase in ΔK48-polyUb persisted at 24 hr of treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: JNJ-26854165-treated S phase cells showed a temporary superlinear increase in degradation at 8 hr but not at 24 hr of treatment.
source: JNJ-26854165-treated S phase cells showed a temporary superlinear increase in degradation at 8 hr but not at 24 hr of treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: CDK2-inhibited cells had a similar level of proteasomes per unit mass as control.
source: These measurements showed that CDK2-inhibited cells had a similar level of proteasomes per unit mass as control (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 5), suggesting that the total number of proteasomes per cell increases proportionally with cell size in CDK2-inhibited cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: A fraction of the intracellular proteasomes are catalytically inactive and can be stimulated in response to stress.
source: It was reported that a fraction of the intracellular proteasomes are catalytically inactive and can be stimulated in response to stress (Collins and Goldberg, 2017; Livneh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There is a linear correlation between cell size and levels of active proteasomes (R = 0.90).
source: These data revealed a linear correlation between cell size and levels of active proteasomes (R = 0.90), suggesting that large cells have proportionately higher levels of active proteasomes (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: The proteasome inhibitor, bortezomib, eliminated the dependence of active proteasomes on cell size.
source: As a positive control, the proteasome inhibitor, bortezomib, eliminated the dependence of active proteasomes on cell size.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Larger cells have proportionally higher levels of active proteasomes, yet exhibit a superlinear increase in K48-polyUb degradation, suggesting that the efficiency of protein degradation per active proteasome may be enhanced.
source: The observation that larger cells have proportionally higher levels of active proteasomes, yet exhibit a superlinear increase in K48-polyUb degradation, suggests that the efficiency of protein degradation per active proteasome may be enhanced, warranting further investigation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: An increased degradation efficiency might be achieved through increased efficiency in protein ubiquitination, such as activating E3 ubiquitin ligases that target proteins for degradation.
source: An increased degradation efficiency might be achieved through increased efficiency in protein ubiquitination, such as activating E3 ubiquitin ligases that target proteins for degradation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Nascent proteins, or newly synthesized polypeptides, are actively degraded in eukaryotic cells as part of protein quality control.
source: Previous studies have shown that nascent proteins, or newly synthesized polypeptides, are actively degraded in eukaryotic cells as part of protein quality control (Wolff et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Up to 15% of nascent chains in human cells are tagged for degradation.
source: It has been estimated that up to 15% of nascent chains in human cells are tagged for degradation (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CHX treatment significantly reduced ΔK48-polyUb levels.
source: As anticipated, CHX treatment significantly reduced ΔK48-polyUb levels (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6), confirming that nascent proteins contribute substantially to proteasomal degradation (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6, and citation to previous work.

claim: In the absence of CHX, CDK2 inhibition resulted in significant increases in ΔK48-polyUb across the cell cycle.
source: In the absence of CHX, CDK2 inhibition resulted in significant increases in ΔK48-polyUb across the cell cycle (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6), consistent with previous results.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: In the presence of CHX, the increase in ΔK48-polyUb was primarily observed at the G1/S transition.
source: However, in the presence of CHX, the increase in ΔK48-polyUb was primarily observed at the G1/S transition (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Cells at the G1/S transition exhibit the highest ΔK48-polyUb levels in both control and CDK2-inhibited cells.
source: Strikingly, cells at the G1/S transition exhibit the highest ΔK48-polyUb levels in both control and CDK2-inhibited cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Rates of global protein degradation observed in large G1/S cells surpassed those of similarly sized or even larger cells in S and G2 phases.
source: Remarkably, rates of global protein degradation observed in these large G1/S cells surpassed those of similarly sized or even larger cells in S and G2 phases, suggesting a hyperactivation of global protein degradation at the G1/S transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The analysis revealed a subpopulation of exceptionally large cells at the G1/S transition, often comparable in size or even larger than cells in S and G2 phases.
source: Interestingly, the analysis revealed a subpopulation of exceptionally large cells at the G1/S transition, often comparable in size or even larger than cells in S and G2 phases (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Time-lapse imaging confirmed that large G1/S cells were not arrested but continued to progress through the cell cycle.
source: Time-lapse imaging confirmed that large G1/S cells were not arrested but continued to progress through the cell cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Large G1/S cells exhibited high levels of ΔK48-polyUb per cell.
source: These large G1/S cells exhibited high levels of ΔK48-polyUb per cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and importantly, the highest levels of ΔK48-polyUb per unit mass (Figure 4E), further supporting the notion of hyperactive protein degradation in large G1/S cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4E.

claim: Large G1/S cells exhibited the highest levels of ΔK48-polyUb per unit mass.
source: These large G1/S cells exhibited high levels of ΔK48-polyUb per cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and importantly, the highest levels of ΔK48-polyUb per unit mass (Figure 4E), further supporting the notion of hyperactive protein degradation in large G1/S cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Under control conditions, large cells on average grew faster than small cells, both before and after the G1/S transition.
source: Under control conditions, large cells on average grew faster than small cells, both before and after the G1/S transition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and when averaged across the entire cell cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), likely due to their higher protein synthesis rates (Figure 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Upon mTOR inhibition, the cellular growth rates of small and large cells converged before the G1/S transition but not after.
source: However, upon mTOR inhibition, the cellular growth rates of small and large cells converged before the G1/S transition but not after (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The convergence of growth rates occurred despite a proportional decrease in protein synthesis rates by mTOR inhibition for all cells, with large cells continuing to synthesize proteins faster than small cells.
source: This convergence occurred despite a proportional decrease in protein synthesis rates by mTOR inhibition for all cells, with large cells continuing to synthesize proteins faster than small cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Large cells prior to the G1/S transition exhibit elevated rates of protein degradation, which counterbalance the higher protein synthesis rates in large cells.
source: These results provide additional evidence that large cells prior to the G1/S transition exhibit elevated rates of protein degradation, which counterbalance the higher protein synthesis rates in large cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Large cells exhibit elevated rates of protein degradation throughout interphase, with a particularly pronounced increase in large cells at the G1/S transition.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate that large cells exhibit elevated rates of protein degradation throughout interphase, with a particularly pronounced increase in large cells at the G1/S transition.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The mechanism of elevated protein degradation in large cells may function in conjunction with the cell size checkpoints to promote cell size uniformity.
source: This mechanism may function in conjunction with the cell size checkpoints to promote cell size uniformity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the function of the mechanism.

claim: Cell size is fundamental to cellular physiology as it sets the scale for subcellular compartments, biosynthetic capacity, and cellular function.
source: Cell size is fundamental to cellular physiology as it sets the scale for subcellular compartments, biosynthetic capacity, and cellular function.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell biology that is part of the study's background.

claim: Evidence of cell size control has been reported from single-celled yeasts to multicellular animals and plants.
source: Evidence of cell size control has been reported from single-celled yeasts to multicellular animals and plants (Dolznig et al., 2004; Hartwell et al., 1974; Neufeld et al., 1998; Nurse, 1975; Willis et al., 2016; Xie and Skotheim, 2020; Zetterberg and Killander, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The precision with which size is controlled manifests in the cell size regularity observed in healthy tissues.
source: The precision with which size is controlled also manifests in the cell size regularity observed in healthy tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell biology that is part of the study's background.

claim: Deregulation of size control often signals cancerous growth as many tumors display increased heterogeneity in cell size.
source: In contrast, deregulation of size control often signals cancerous growth as many tumors display increased heterogeneity in cell size (Asadullah et al., 2021; Bell and Waizbard, 1986; Lee et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies on cell size control have predominantly focused on cell size checkpoints, in that a critical size threshold is required for cell cycle progression.
source: Previous studies on cell size control have predominantly focused on cell size checkpoints, in that a critical size threshold is required for cell cycle progression (D'Ario et al., 2021; Ginzberg et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Sellam et al., 2019; Zatulovskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Size-dependent compensatory growth functions independently of cell cycle checkpoints.
source: In this study, we investigated size-dependent compensatory growth, which functions independently of cell cycle checkpoints.
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of the study.

claim: The rates of global protein synthesis and degradation increase with cell size in both perturbed and unperturbed conditions.
source: We found that the rates of global protein synthesis and degradation increase with cell size in both perturbed and unperturbed conditions (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Protein synthesis rates scaled proportionally with cell size, but protein degradation rates were disproportionately higher in large CDK2-inhibited cells.
source: Interestingly, although protein synthesis rates scaled proportionally with cell size, protein degradation rates were disproportionately higher in large CDK2-inhibited cells (i.e., higher rates of protein degradation per unit mass), suggesting active upregulation of the proteasomal degradation pathway (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: CDK4/6 inhibition, which induces a larger target size without triggering compensatory growth slowdown, exhibited the same linear scaling between cell size and protein degradation rates as in control.
source: In contrast, CDK4/6 inhibition, which induces a larger target size without triggering compensatory growth slowdown, exhibited the same linear scaling between cell size and protein degradation rates as in control (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Perturbations that forced overgrowth in cell size by extending S or G2/M phases induced superlinear increases in protein degradation.
source: We also tested two other perturbations that forced overgrowth in cell size by extending S or G2/M phases. Like CDK2 inhibition, these perturbations induced superlinear increases in protein degradation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting that activation of protein degradation functions as a general compensatory mechanism of cell size control in response to prolonged growth periods, irrespective of the specific cell cycle stage affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Analysis across the cell cycle highlighted a particularly striking increase in global protein degradation in large cells at the G1/S transition.
source: Further analysis across the cell cycle highlighted a particularly striking increase in global protein degradation in large cells at the G1/S transition (Figure 4), consistent with the stringent size control observed at the G1 exit (Ginzberg et al., 2018; Zetterberg and Killander, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4 and citations to previous work.

claim: Large polyploid cells in a cancerous mouse lymphocytic leukemia cell line do not reduce growth efficiency compared to smaller diploid cells.
source: While this study focused on human RPE1 cells, a non-cancerous epithelial cell line, previous work (Mu et al., 2020) on a cancerous mouse lymphocytic leukemia cell line found that large polyploid cells do not reduce growth efficiency compared to smaller diploid cells, suggesting that growth rate regulation may be cell type- and ploidy-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Small cells may accelerate their growth at certain cell cycle stages.
source: Previous work has also suggested that small cells may accelerate their growth at certain cell cycle stages (Cadart et al., 2018; Ginzberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: High-throughput screens on both animal cells and yeasts identified that small cells activate the stress-responding p38 MAPK (Hog1) pathway to prolong the cell cycle.
source: High-throughput screens on both animal cells and yeasts identified that small cells activate the stress-responding p38 MAPK (Hog1) pathway to prolong the cell cycle (Liu et al., 2018; Sellam et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activation of the p38 pathway by osmotic stress results in reduced protein degradation and lower proteasome activity.
source: Previous work on p38 also found that activation of the pathway by osmotic stress results in reduced protein degradation and lower proteasome activity (Lee et al., 2010), whereas p38 inhibition significantly promoted proteasome activity (Leestemaker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: p38 inhibition significantly promoted proteasome activity.
source: Previous work on p38 also found that activation of the pathway by osmotic stress results in reduced protein degradation and lower proteasome activity (Lee et al., 2010), whereas p38 inhibition significantly promoted proteasome activity (Leestemaker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The p38 MAPK activation in small cells may function in both the cell size checkpoint and growth rate regulation.
source: These reports suggest an intriguing possibility that the p38 MAPK activation in small cells may function in both the cell size checkpoint and growth rate regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from previous work.

claim: The G1/S transition may serve as a critical regulatory point for protein degradation and growth rate control.
source: This suggests that, in addition to accommodating cell size checkpoints, the G1/S transition may also serve as a critical regulatory point for protein degradation and growth rate control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Previous observations showed decreased variability in both cell size and growth rate at the G1/S transition.
source: These findings align with previous observation of decreased variability in both cell size and growth rate at the G1/S transition (Ginzberg et al., 2018; Kafri et al., 2013; Son et al., 2012; Zetterberg and Killander, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Progression through the cell cycle, including the G1/S and G2/M transitions, is controlled by ubiquitin-mediated degradation of cell cycle regulators.
source: It is well established that progression through the cell cycle, including the G1/S and G2/M transitions, is controlled by ubiquitin-mediated degradation of cell cycle regulators (Barr et al., 2016; Nakayama and Nakayama, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both nascent proteins and long-lived proteins are targeted for degradation during compensatory growth slowdown, with the relative contribution of each depending on the cell cycle stage.
source: We also found that both nascent proteins and long-lived proteins are targeted for degradation during compensatory growth slowdown, with the relative contribution of each depending on the cell cycle stage (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Cells leverage the proteasomal degradation pathway of nascent chains to modulate their growth rate and maintain cell size homeostasis.
source: While proteasomal degradation of nascent chains is classically associated with protein quality control, our data suggest that cells leverage this pathway to modulate their growth rate and maintain cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Proteasome subunits were found at higher concentrations in large cells.
source: Two recent studies Cheng et al., 2021; Lanz et al., 2021 used such an approach and measured individual protein concentrations in cells of different sizes. Proteasome subunits were found at higher concentrations in large cells, consistent with elevated rates of ubiquitylation and protein turnover.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Components involved in translation show slightly reduced concentrations in large cells.
source: Interestingly, components involved in translation show slightly reduced concentrations in large cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from cited studies.

claim: Oversized cells in yeast show impaired gene expression.
source: Previous work in yeast Neurohr et al., 2019 demonstrated that oversized cells show impaired gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: If translation integrity is disrupted in large cells, increased levels of ubiquitin-mediated degradation may be required for the clearance of aberrant nascent polypeptides through protein quality control pathways.
source: If translation integrity is disrupted in large cells, increased levels of ubiquitin-mediated degradation may be required for the clearance of aberrant nascent polypeptides through protein quality control pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference.

claim: Compensatory growth can be employed in the homeostatic size control of nonproliferating cells.
source: Our findings provide mechanistic insight into the process of compensatory growth which, unlike cell size checkpoints, can be employed in the homeostatic size control of nonproliferating cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Maintaining cells within their optimal size range is crucial for cellular and organ function.
source: Maintaining cells within their optimal size range is crucial for cellular and organ function.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell biology that is part of the study's background.

claim: In adipocytes, the release of fatty acid induced by epinephrine was found to be highly dependent on the cell surface area.
source: In adipocytes, the release of fatty acid induced by epinephrine was found to be highly dependent on the cell surface area (Zinder and Shapiro, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pancreatic beta cells undergoing hypertrophy show enhanced insulin secretion and improved glucose homeostasis in vivo.
source: Pancreatic beta cells undergoing hypertrophy show enhanced insulin secretion and improved glucose homeostasis in vivo (Helman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cells dynamically control their size to modulate cell- and tissue-level functions in response to physiological demand.
source: Across tissue types, cells dynamically control their size to modulate cell- and tissue-level functions in response to physiological demand; these include compensatory hypertrophy in pancreatic and hepatic cells (Dhawan et al., 2007; Ginzberg et al., 2015; Miettinen et al., 2014), compensatory renal cell hypertrophy following nephrectomy (Rojas-Canales et al., 2019) or increased urine flow (Boehlke et al., 2010), growth of neurons (axons) in coordination with animal development (Albus et al., 2013), and the likely regulation of functional mass of the hormone-secreting glands in response to stress (Karin et al., 2020; Karin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.
